title: Find a hidden coolant leak with an inspection mirror and mark the spot above it
instruction: Using the inspection mirror, find where coolant has leaked on the housing's hidden side face inside the gap, then mark that spot with the paint marker on the cover strip directly above it. Do not let the mirror touch the hidden face, and put both tools down when you are done.
context: Done by: general maintenance and repair workers (about 1.6 million US jobs) and automotive service technicians and mechanics (805,600), BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook 2024. O*NET 49-9071.00 task: "Inspect, operate, or test machinery or equipment to diagnose machine malfunctions." O*NET 49-3023.00 task: "Inspect vehicles for damage and record findings so that necessary repairs can be made." A leak on a face that sits close to a wall is found with a hand inspection mirror and its place marked for the repair.
setup: Station table; x forward from the line between the arm bases, y left, heights above the table top. A grey steel housing side and a dark wall (18 x 13 cm, 5 mm steel) stand 60 mm apart from x 22.5 to 40.5 cm, the gap centred on y 0; it is open at its near end (facing the robot), closed at the far end and the bottom, and on top by a 70 mm wide, 5 mm steel cover strip (top 13.5 cm up) that sits on two locating pins and is held by two M5 thumb screws, one at each end. The housing's face inside the gap (the hidden face) is painted light grey. On it, the coolant trace: a dry, printed green patch, 22 x 50 mm, cut from a removable matte white paper label sheet (Avery 6465, about 0.1 mm thick) printed solid green on a laser printer; centred 7.5 cm up, at one of five places x 30, 32, 34, 36 or 38 cm, 7.5 to 15.5 cm in from the open end (drawn per trial from the seed). Before each trial the whole face, patch included, gets a light coat of white marking chalk (IRWIN STRAIT-LINE, white) as a contact witness: any touch wipes it. Ullman HTC-2LT lighted telescoping inspection mirror, off the shelf (maker's product page: 2-3/8 in (60 mm) round glass mirror, built-in LED powered by two CR2016 cells in a black plastic case behind the glass, telescopes 10 to 37 in (254 to 940 mm), 4.5 oz (128 g)); light on; head set at 45 degrees on its joint, hanging below the shaft, glass facing the robot and the hidden face; black cushioned grip 100 mm long, 12.7 mm across; steel shaft out 120 mm past the grip: grip on two support blocks (6061 aluminium bar, grey anodised, 12 x 30 x 94 mm, taped to the table with double-sided foam tape) at (12.5, -13) and (22.5, -13) cm, its free end (x 11.5 cm) toward the robot. Sharpie oil-based paint marker, medium point (142 x 16 mm, 22 g, yellow paint): standing tip down in a steel pen cup (34 mm square, 60 mm tall, 18 mm bore) on a 50 mm steel stand at (19, 9) cm. Both grippers open at the ready pose, pads clean (see reset notes).
scoring: Contact: if anything touches the hidden face anywhere (x 22.5 to 40.5 cm, table to strip): any part of the mirror (glass, back, rim, joint, shaft or grip, wherever the head is), the marker or any part of the robot, the score is 0 for the rest of the trial, even after an earlier scored rest (touching: within 0.25 mm, the simulator's resting-contact gap). Paint mark: where the marker tip touches the strip's top face (within 0.25 mm; a hover makes no mark); a touch more than 3 mm from every earlier mark makes a new mark. Pause: the mirror head's centre in the gap with the head moving under 1 cm/s and the mirror turning under 0.1 rad/s, for 0.5 s or more. Seen: a wrist camera sees the trace's middle (16 x 30 mm: its centre and points 8 mm to each side and 15 mm above and below) reflected at least 1.5 mm inside the glass's edge and inside the image, the glass facing both the camera and the trace, with nothing (housing, tools, robot) blocking either leg of the view. Look: a mark counts only if the last pause before it ended with the trace seen for 0.5 s without a break; otherwise it earns 0. Per mark (after a look): 1.0 if its centre is within 6 mm (along the gap) of the trace's centre, falling linearly to 0 at 14 mm. Score = the lowest mark credit (a stray mark sends the repair to the wrong place); 0 with no mark. The score takes that value when both tools have been put down for 1 s: each still (under 1 cm/s and 0.1 rad/s), released (no part of the robot within 5 mm of it) and off the housing, with both grippers at least 80% open; a new mark lowers the score at once. 1.0 ends the trial. Real trial: measure the mark from a plumb line off the trace with a tape measure. Look: in the wrist camera footage, the last time the mirror was held still in the gap before the mark (the trace's image shifting less than a quarter of its 22 mm width over 0.5 s), the trace's middle must be inside the mirror's glass for 0.5 s, or the score is 0. Contact: lift the strip after the trial and photograph the face; any wipe in the chalk (on the face or on the patch) not in the reference photo taken before the trial, or chalk on the mirror, the marker or the robot's finger pads (pressed on a black card), scores 0. Put down: top camera footage shows each tool still for 1 s, off the housing, with no part of the robot touching it.
reset_notes: Loosen the two thumb screws and lift the cover strip straight up off its pins: the gap is then open from above. Off the rig, wipe the strip's paint marks off with a rag and mineral spirits and let it dry. Brush the old chalk off the face with a dry, soft 25 mm brush and wipe it with a dry microfibre cloth: no liquid on the rig. Peel off the old patch and stick a fresh one at the place drawn for the trial, centred at that x and 7.5 cm up (five scribe lines on the housing's top edge, hidden under the strip, mark the places). With a sheet of paper on the table under the gap, dust the whole face, patch included, with a light coat of the chalk from the brush; tap the housing once and take the paper away. Photograph the face square-on (the reference photo; the green must show clearly). Put the strip back and tighten the screws. Pads: chalk is only inside the gap, put on with the strip off and the robot at its ready pose, so a pad meets it only by touching the face (score 0). The patch is dry; the only wet paint is the marker's tip and marks, and the pads hold the barrel about 75 mm above the tip. Before each trial, wipe each pad, the mirror and the marker barrel with a dry microfibre cloth, then with a lint-free wipe damp with 70% isopropyl alcohol; let dry 1 minute and press each pad on a black card: no white or yellow mark. Lay the mirror back on its two blocks (grip toward the robot, head set at 45 degrees, light on) and stand the marker tip down in its cup.
fidelity: Ideal flat mirror, reflective on the glass only; joint fixed at 45 degrees; the HTC-2LT's LED lights the face; grip square in section; case thickness and marker mass estimated. Trace: a 22 x 50 mm green film, as the printed patch. Contact and release use exact distances between whole convex solids (mirror, marker, robot collision boxes) and the hidden face; touching = within 0.25 mm. A real chalk witness shows any touch. The look uses reflection geometry from the wrist cameras.
scores: Dream-1 run, seed 0: 0.0 (3,600 steps). Scripted demo, reading the hidden face in the mirror from the wrist cameras: 1.0 on seeds 0, 1 and 2 (1,283 steps each). Wrong outcomes: mirror touches the face 0.0; marked without looking 0.0; looked but marked the wrong place 0.0.
